title: CWG Gold Medallist Harsh Singh Seeks Japan Training Ahead of Asian Games
excerpt: India's first male judo Commonwealth Games gold medallist wants to train under Olympic-level coaches in Japan or Georgia before competing at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games next month.
body:
• Judoka Harsh Singh, who became India's first male Commonwealth Games gold medallist in judo at Glasgow, is targeting training stints in Japan or Georgia ahead of the Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya
  • Singh acknowledged that Asian Games competition is significantly tougher than the Commonwealth Games and said Indian judokas need to improve technique, footwork and gripping
  • The Asian Games, set for next month, represent a major step up for Singh as he aims to translate his CWG success onto a bigger international stage

Harsh Singh has already made history. Now the judoka wants to build on it. The first Indian male to win a Commonwealth Games gold medal in judo, Singh has set his sights on the Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya next month — and believes overseas training is the key to competing at that level.

"I want to go to Japan or Georgia. These two countries are ideal for Indian judokas," Singh told PTI on the sidelines of a felicitation ceremony for judokas. "Along with Japan, Georgia is one of the strongest nations in judo. Training there will be very beneficial for our future preparation."

Bridging the Technical Gap

Singh was candid about the distance between Indian judo and the sport's global elite. While he praised the physical strength of Indian athletes, he said technical deficiencies remain a significant barrier.

"Japanese coaches are strong in terms of experience and technique. We Indians are strong but we are a little behind in terms of technique. Footwork, and a bit more gripping — if we improve in these aspects, we will be able to perform better."

— Harsh Singh

The request to train abroad has not yet been formally submitted, Singh said, but he expressed hope that exposure to coaches who have achieved Olympic success could elevate India's judo programme to the next level.

Glasgow Gold, Asian Games Challenge

Singh's Commonwealth Games gold in Glasgow was a milestone for Indian judo. India had previously won silver and bronze in the discipline, but never gold on the men's side. Singh said he had entered the competition with the gold medal as his only target.

"India has won silver and bronze before. So, I was looking for gold. I was preparing for that," he said. "If we practice well and go with a positive mindset, we can win gold."

He recounted his semifinal bout as the toughest of the competition, describing how he adapted his strategy after finding that his opponent used a similar style. A technique called Kataguruma — a shoulder throw involving pulling the opponent down and driving them onto the mat — proved decisive in the final.

A Harder Road Ahead

Singh was forthright about the gulf in competition levels. "When one compares the Commonwealth Games with the Asian Games or the Olympics, it's a little easier to get a medal in judo," he said. The Asian Games field includes athletes from Japan, South Korea, Mongolia and the Central Asian nations — all traditional judo powerhouses with deep competitive traditions.

For Singh, the Aichi-Nagoya Games represent both an opportunity and a test of whether his Glasgow success can translate to a stage where India has historically struggled. His preferred technique, Tomoe Nage — a sacrifice throw that is his signature move — will face opponents trained in the sport's most demanding environments.

Diaspora Interest in Indian Combat Sports

Singh's trajectory reflects the growing profile of Indian combat sports beyond cricket, drawing attention from diaspora sports fans tracking the country's progress in Olympic disciplines. A strong Asian Games performance could further raise judo's profile among the Indian sporting public and strengthen the case for sustained investment in overseas training for Indian martial arts athletes.
